reading.body:
No generative AI medical device has a settled regulatory path. The FDA has asked for public input on how to regulate devices built on generative models, whose outputs vary and are hard to validate exhaustively. The first clearance of software built on a large language model for clinical care was announced in 2026.

The FDA's discussion paper is not guidance and sets no requirements. That distinction matters: a request for feedback signals the agency has not decided how to handle outputs that change between runs. Traditional device review assumes a fixed function that can be tested the same way twice. A generative model does not offer that, so the validation question stays open.

The UpDoc clearance shows a path exists, not that it is settled. One clearance does not establish what reviewers will accept next, and the data does not say what the FDA required of it. For a medtech team, the practical implication is to constrain what a generative device may say and test it against adversarial and out of scope inputs, because that is where reviewers will press.

What this does not cover: the data gives no detail on the UpDoc submission, no predicate device, no clearance pathway, and no European counterpart. It also does not say how many generative device submissions are pending. The regulatory picture here rests on one discussion paper and one clearance.

terms.line: The field of computer science dedicated to creating systems that perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence: understanding language, recognizing patterns, making decisions.
A generative model trained on vast text corpora, capable of understanding, summarizing, generating, and predicting language.

Models that create new content, text, images, video, audio, code, from patterns learned in training data. The 2022 shift from AI that classifies to AI that produces is what put this glossary on your reading list.
The 2026 package of targeted amendments to the EU AI Act, deferring high-risk deadlines and restructuring conformity assessment.

A generative model confidently outputting false, fabricated, or unsupported information. The fluency is the danger: fabricated content arrives in the same authoritative voice as fact, which is why verification belongs in every AI workflow.

explainer:
Most AI devices so far are narrow: they detect a finding on an image or classify a signal, and their outputs can be tested against a reference standard. Generative AI devices are different. Built on large language or multimodal models, they produce text, summaries or recommendations that vary from one run to the next and can cover open ended situations, which makes exhaustive testing impossible and hallucination a real risk.

Regulators are working out how to handle this. The FDA has published a discussion paper and sought public input on topics such as how to describe intended use for flexible models, how to evaluate performance and hallucination, how to manage updates to underlying models and what transparency users need. Developers in this space typically narrow the intended use, constrain outputs to defined tasks, test heavily against adversarial and out of scope inputs, and keep a clinician reviewing every output.

What makes a generative device different

Most approved AI devices give a bounded output: a probability, a measurement, a flag. A generative device produces open ended content, such as a draft radiology report, a summary of a patient's record, an answer to a clinician's question or a plan. The space of possible outputs is effectively unlimited, which breaks the usual approach of testing every output class. It also means the device can produce confident, fluent errors that look like correct clinical content.

Where regulators stand

The FDA has said that generative AI intended for medical purposes can be a device, and that it is working out how to evaluate products whose outputs cannot be enumerated. It has held public discussions on the topic and has described the challenges: evaluating performance when every output is different, handling models that change, managing uses outside the intended purpose, and understanding how clinicians actually rely on the outputs. As of now, authorised generative devices are few and narrowly scoped, and much of what is marketed sits in categories the FDA does not regulate as devices, such as some documentation and administrative tools.

What manufacturers are doing

Those pursuing authorisation are narrowing the intended use tightly, constraining the model with retrieval from verified sources and with output checks, testing on large samples of real cases with expert review of each output, measuring how often clinicians catch the errors that occur, and designing the product so the clinician reviews and edits rather than accepts. They are also preparing for post market monitoring of outputs at scale, because a generative device is the clearest case where performance in the field cannot be assumed from the test set.
